title: Piezoacoustic recirculating delay loops stream decode weights, skipping DRAM
idea: LLM decode reads every weight in the same fixed order each token, so a bank of GHz LiNbO3 bulk-acoustic delay loops on the interposer holds weight shards as circulating phonon pulses. The pulses are re-amplified each lap and timed to arrive exactly when the systolic array needs them. Piezo transducers convert bits to acoustic packets at ~10 Gb/s per loop, and thousands of loops form a sequential 'weight carousel'.
why: Takes deterministic weight streams out of DRAM: no row activations and no overfetch (facts 5, 8). Target is 20-40% less DRAM for small-batch inference, but each loop holds only ~10-100 kb, so it suits on-package buffers.

title: Pyroelectric film images row heat to steer page tiering
idea: Deposit a thin LiTaO3 pyroelectric layer over each DRAM bank, patterned into per-subarray pixels. Activation bursts heat their rows by millikelvins; each pixel emits charge proportional to dT/dt, and a tiny integrator turns that into a hotness map. The OS keeps only the hottest 20-30% of pages in DRAM and pushes cold pages to compressed CXL or flash, with no SRAM access counters or page-table sampling.
why: Gives tiering hardware-free access tracking. Cuts DRAM per server 30-40% for <1% area and no extra periphery (fact 7).

title: Mott-oscillator phase locking flags duplicate pages for inline dedup
idea: Each page fingerprint drives a row of NbO2 threshold-switch relaxation oscillators through bit-weighted coupling resistors. Rows fed identical patterns injection-lock in phase within ~100 cycles, while different patterns stay incoherent. One phase detector therefore answers 'does this page duplicate any of N stored signatures?' in parallel, and a hit triggers copy-on-write page merging in the hypervisor.
why: Dedup across VMs and containers saves 15-40% of DRAM in cloud hosts. The all-to-all compare costs O(1) energy instead of hashing and searching on every write.

title: Coulomb-blockade charge packets store 3-bit KV and compute attention
idea: Store each KV element as an integer number of electrons (0-7) on silicon nanodots, where the Coulomb staircase quantizes charge natively. A key column's packets are merged onto a shared island and a single-electron transistor counts the electrons, giving the attention dot product. Physics enforces 3-bit quantization, so no codec is needed.
why: Shrinks the KV cache ~5x versus FP16, and scores never leave the array (facts 5, 8). Speculative: room-temperature blockade needs dots under 3 nm.

title: Tunneling-leak gain cells make old KV tokens fade like ALiBi
idea: Store KV entries in gain cells whose tunneling oxide is deliberately thin, so charge decays with a time constant of a few hundred tokens. Each read value is then naturally scaled by exp(-age/tau), which is exactly a recency-bias attention prior. Cells whose signal drops below the sense threshold are reclaimed as free slots, with no refresh or eviction logic.
why: Gives refresh-free KV memory (fact 3) that reclaims its own capacity. Expect a 3-8x smaller KV footprint for long contexts, where distant tokens are down-weighted anyway.

title: Spin-Hall stochastic writes keep an attention-weighted KV reservoir
idea: When a token's KV arrives, a spin-Hall (beta-W) current pulse tries to switch a low-barrier MTJ, with amplitude set by the token's running attention score. The switching probability equals the keep probability, so the KV buffer becomes a hardware importance-weighted reservoir sample of the context. Only switched tokens are written to the fixed-size KV store; dropped ones are compensated by unbiased reweighting.
why: Caps KV memory at a fixed budget (4-10x smaller) while keeping attention estimates unbiased. One device per token replaces digital PRNG and sort logic.

title: Electrochromic WO3 shutters hold model weights inside the photonic multiplier
idea: Each weight is a Li-intercalated WO3 attenuator on a silicon-nitride waveguide mesh. An ion-injection pulse sets its optical transmission once, and it holds without power. Activations ride on light and are multiplied as they pass through the colored film, so the weights live in the compute fabric and DRAM holds only activations and KV.
why: Weight-stationary optics takes both weight capacity and weight traffic out of DRAM (fact 5). That means 50-90% less DRAM for inference appliances whose models rarely change.

title: Photoconductive receivers let one optical broadcast replace replicated weight copies
idea: Today every GPU's HBM holds an identical weight copy for data-parallel inference. Instead, a single master copy is broadcast over waveguide or free-space optics to dozens of compute dies. Each die captures the bits just in time with photoconductive Ge sampling receivers and keeps only a small staging buffer.
why: Replication is often 4-16x the model size per cluster. Broadcast cuts that DRAM/HBM to about one copy plus buffers (facts 5, 6).

title: Silver-ion drift integrators remember page heat across reboots
idea: Every 64 KB region gets a nanoscale Ag/electrolyte integrator. Each access pulse drifts a few silver ions, so conductance becomes a nonvolatile, slowly relaxing log of cumulative accesses. On boot or VM migration, the placement engine reads the map and pre-places hot data in DRAM and cold data in CXL/flash right away, instead of relearning for minutes.
why: Tiering is accurate from second zero, so providers can provision 20-30% less DRAM without cold-start penalties.

title: Spin-orbit domain-wall racetrack serves the append-only KV cache
idea: The KV cache is written only at its tail and read in full order every decode step, which is exactly a racetrack's access pattern. SOT current pulses shift magnetic domain walls along nanowires, appending each new token at the write head and streaming all tokens past a read head once per step. No random-access decoders or row activations are needed.
why: At ~1-2F^2 per bit with no refresh, the KV tier costs 3-5x less per bit than DRAM (facts 1, 3, 8).

title: CCD bucket-brigade wells store transient activations as analog charge
idea: Write inter-layer activations as analog charge packets into a buried-channel CCD shift register, one packet per value at 5-6 effective bits. The packets are clocked bucket-brigade style to the consuming layer. Activations are consumed within microseconds, so dark-current loss is negligible and neither refresh nor an ADC is needed before use.
why: One ~2F^2 charge well replaces 8-16 DRAM bits per activation, about 4-8x density for transient data (facts 1, 4).

title: Fourier lens compresses training activation checkpoints at light speed
idea: Activation tiles saved for backprop are loaded onto a spatial light modulator, and a lens computes their 2D Fourier transform in one pass. A thresholding camera keeps only the high-energy coefficients (JPEG-style) for storage. Inverse optics, or a cheap digital IFFT, restores them during the backward pass.
why: Activations are 60-80% of training memory. Lossy 8-20x compression with a free transform shrinks the HBM requirement (facts 5, 6).

title: Photorefractive hologram recalls top-k keys so values stay offloaded
idea: All keys of a long context are written as superimposed holograms in an Fe:LiNbO3 crystal. Shining the current query beam reconstructs correlation peaks whose brightness equals each query-key dot product, all in parallel, and a camera picks the top-k tokens. Only those k values are fetched from flash or CXL, so the bulk KV never sits in DRAM.
why: Long-context KV caches of hundreds of GB move to cheap tiers, and DRAM holds only the top-k working set, roughly 10-50x less (facts 5, 8).

title: Stochastic-resonance multi-reads recover bits from undersized gain cells
idea: For error-tolerant data (images, embeddings, low-order weight bits), shrink storage nodes to ~1 fF in a gain-cell array with non-destructive reads. Add calibrated noise to the sense reference and average 4-8 fast reads; the dither lifts the sub-threshold signal across the decision line (stochastic resonance), giving acceptable bit-error rates.
why: Creates a 'lossy tier' needing 4x less stored charge, which sidesteps the capacitor wall (fact 1). Gives 2-3x density on the ~40% of data that tolerates errors.

title: Magnonic interference hashes KV keys to merge near-duplicate tokens
idea: Key vectors are injected as microwave phases into a YIG spin-wave interferometer whose fixed geometry implements a random projection. Output-port intensities give locality-sensitive hash bits in nanoseconds. Tokens that land in the same bucket are merged into one averaged KV entry with a count, so redundant context collapses.
why: Long contexts are highly redundant: merging cuts KV memory 2-5x, and spin-wave hashing costs only aJ-scale energy (fact 5).

title: Resonant-tunneling diodes decompress memory lines inline at line rate
idea: Put a multi-valued logic block of InGaAs/AlAs resonant-tunneling diodes (negative differential resistance, 100+ GHz) on the memory channel. Every 64-byte line can then be stored compressed (base-delta or entropy-coded) and expanded within one memory clock. With no latency penalty, the OS has no reason to keep any data uncompressed.
why: Transparent compression gives 1.5-2x effective capacity across all memory, not just cold pages (fact 5).

title: Pockels thin-film lithium niobate links make rack memory pooling viable
idea: Use thin-film LiNbO3 Pockels modulators (sub-pJ/bit, no carrier lifetime, ns latency) in CXL optical links so a rack-scale memory pool sits under 100 ns away. Servers keep a small local DRAM and borrow from the pool on demand, which removes per-server overprovisioning.
why: Stranded memory runs 25-35% in cloud fleets. Pooling recovers most of it, so each rack buys ~20% less DRAM.

title: Charge-trap flash computes attention over cold tokens in place
idea: KV tokens older than a recency window are programmed by Fowler-Nordheim tunneling into charge-trap NAND strings as analog conductances. The query is applied as wordline voltages, and bitline currents sum the dot products, so the array returns only the attention-weighted value sum. DRAM keeps just the last few thousand tokens.
why: KV for 1M-token contexts lives in NAND bits that are ~10x cheaper, and the DRAM KV footprint drops 10-100x (facts 4, 5).

title: Charge sharing rebuilds rows from a base row plus deltas
idea: Store groups of similar rows (neighboring embedding vectors, image tiles) as one full-precision base row plus low-bit delta rows. On read, the subarray opens the base and delta rows together onto shared bitlines with binary-weighted capacitive coupling, so charge redistribution adds them in analog before sensing. Decompression happens inside the mat with no logic.
why: Gives 1.5-3x effective capacity for redundant data at zero periphery cost (facts 7, 8).

title: Acousto-optic steered holographic cube as microsecond tier below DRAM
idea: A TeO2 acousto-optic deflector steers a laser to any of ~10^5 page holograms in a photopolymer cube within ~5 us. Each flash reads a 1 Mb page onto a camera chip. Cold but randomly accessed data, such as embedding tables and old KV, lives here instead of DRAM.
why: A dense, cheap page tier between DRAM and SSD lets DRAM shrink 30-50% in embedding-heavy workloads.

title: Fiber speckle random projections shrink recommendation embedding tables
idea: Replace TB-scale embedding tables with compact codes. A thermally stabilized multimode fiber's speckle acts as a fixed, enormous random matrix, so a short per-ID code expands optically into a full embedding (the hashing trick at light speed). Only the codes and a small learned correction table stay in DRAM.
why: Embedding tables are the largest DRAM consumer in recommender clusters. Compresses them 10-50x.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory pool exploits frozen leakage for refresh-free density
idea: At 77 K, thermally activated junction leakage and GIDL fall by more than 10^6, stretching retention from 64 ms to hours. A shared DRAM pool in an LN2 bath can then use 2-3x smaller capacitors and no refresh, and it serves a whole rack over optical links.
why: Both the capacitor wall (fact 1) and refresh (fact 3) disappear, giving ~2x bits per wafer in the pooled tier.

title: Skyrmion reservoir replaces recurrent weights with magnetic dynamics
idea: Input currents excite a Ta/CoFeB/MgO skyrmion fabric whose nonlinear, fading-memory dynamics act as the state transition of a sequence model. A few MTJs read out the state, so only a small linear readout is stored, not large recurrent or state-space matrices.
why: Removes most weight storage from streaming time-series models (sensor fusion, keyword spotting), with 10-100x fewer stored parameters.

title: Scandium-doped AlN FeFETs keep weights resident at 125 C
idea: Store weights as polarization states in AlScN ferroelectric FETs, arranged in a NOR array that performs the MAC in place. With a Curie point above 1000 C and a ~4 MV/cm coercive field, the wurtzite polarization does not depolarize over 10 years at 125 C. DRAM holds only activations.
why: Edge and automotive accelerators drop the LPDDR weight copy (often 60-80% of capacity) and avoid the 4x refresh penalty DRAM pays at 125 C.

title: Buckled AlN micro-beams store compression codebooks with zero leakage
idea: Weight-clustering codebooks and LZ dictionaries (a few hundred KB, rarely updated) are stored as up/down buckled states of AlN-actuated micro-beams next to the decompression engine. A piezo pulse snaps a beam and capacitive sensing reads it. With no charge to leak, 125 C for 10 years is a non-issue, whereas SRAM leaks heavily at that temperature and loses its contents at power-off.
why: The whole model can stay 4-8x compressed in memory with its codebook always on-die, cutting DRAM capacity 3-6x in hot ECUs.

title: Antifuse weight ROM banks rotate through over-the-air model updates
idea: Freeze automotive perception weights into oxide-breakdown antifuse arrays with in-array MAC. Ship 8 banks and burn one per model release, so each OTA update takes a fresh bank. A broken-down oxide filament is permanent at 125 C.
why: ECUs need no DRAM for weights. Antifuse is 28 nm logic-compatible, U.S.-manufacturable and needs no EUV (fact 4).

title: Dispersive SAW chirp lines compress radar data before the ADC
idea: Automotive radars buffer the full range-Doppler cube in DRAM. Instead, an AlN-on-sapphire dispersive SAW delay line does analog pulse compression and range transformation on each chirp, so only range bins above the CFAR threshold are digitized and stored. SAW devices are already qualified to AEC-Q200 at 125 C, and the piezo material is stable far beyond that.
why: Cuts radar DRAM buffering 10-30x and saves ADC power, freeing DRAM in ADAS domain controllers.

title: Phase-change drift doubles as a built-in page age clock
idea: Give each page a Ge-rich GST cell that is reset on access. Structural relaxation makes its resistance drift upward as log(t), so reading the cell tells the controller the time since last use. A co-located reference cell drifts at the same 125 C temperature and normalizes the reading. Eviction to compressed or NVM tiers picks the oldest pages without timestamp SRAM.
why: Cheap, nonvolatile LRU age for every page enables aggressive tiering, with 30-50% less DRAM. Ge-rich GST retains data ~10 years at 150 C.

title: Silicon-carbide gain-cell scratchpad holds activations refresh-free at 125 C
idea: Build the NPU's activation scratchpad from 2T gain cells in 4H-SiC. The 3.26 eV bandgap keeps generation leakage below ~1e-21 A even at 125 C, which gives retention of minutes, so whole-layer activations stay on-die instead of spilling to external DRAM.
why: External DRAM for activations disappears from hot edge and automotive NPUs. The cells need no refresh at temperatures where DRAM needs 4x refresh.

title: Compiler lifetime typing parks short-lived buffers in refresh-free banks
idea: Arrhenius scaling puts DRAM tail retention at 125 C around 8-16 ms. The compiler tags every buffer with its lifetime (activations, per-step KV, DMA staging). Buffers whose producer-consumer gap is under 2 ms go to banks with refresh disabled, and long-lived data goes to robust NVM. On-die canary cells re-check the retention model at every boot over the 10-year life.
why: At 125 C, refresh would eat 20-40% of bandwidth. Turning it off for ~70% of banks recovers that bandwidth, so a smaller DRAM serves the same workload.

title: Peltier-cooled DRAM island inside a 125 C module
idea: Mount one small LPDDR die on a thin-film Bi2Te3 Peltier cooler held at 85 C, and keep the rest of the working set in heat-tolerant NVM (AlScN FeFET or Ge-rich PCM). The cooled island holds only the hottest 10-15% of data, so cooling costs just a few watts.
why: Most data avoids 4x refresh and retention failure at 125 C, and DRAM per ECU drops 5-10x.

title: Lithium niobate domain-wall cells store write-once KV caches
idea: Each KV entry is written once per token and read many times, so store it in thin-film LiNbO3 domain-wall memory. A voltage pulse creates a conductive head-to-head domain wall between electrodes, and reading the wall current is non-destructive. LiNbO3's 1140 C Curie point keeps walls pinned for 10 years at 125 C, and 1e8+ cycles is plenty for one write per session.
why: Nonvolatile, refresh-free KV for in-vehicle LLMs lets prefix caches persist across sessions, and KV leaves DRAM entirely.

title: Straintronic nanomagnets compute bitmap-index logic in place
idea: Store database and feature bitmaps as Galfenol nanomagnet states on an AlN piezo layer. A voltage-induced strain pulse rotates the magnets, and dipole coupling between neighbors computes AND/OR across bit-columns in place, so compressed bitmap indexes are queried without decompressing into DRAM. Galfenol's ~670 C Curie point and shape anisotropy keep the energy barrier above 60 kT at 125 C.
why: Analytics indexes stay compressed and are computed in place, with 5-10x less DRAM for in-vehicle map and feature queries and aJ-scale switching.

title: NbO2 Mott spiking encoders store activations as sparse events
idea: NbO2 Mott threshold-switch oscillators convert layer activations into spike trains. The insulator-metal transition sits near 800 C, so devices stay stable at 125 C ambient. Only spike addresses (typically 5-10% density) are written to memory as event lists, not dense tensors.
why: Activation memory drops 10-20x for sensor-processing networks.

title: Silicon-carbide NEMS relays form leak-free CAM for KV prefix matching
idea: Build a content-addressable memory from SiC nano-electromechanical relays (contacts demonstrated at 500 C) that stores prompt-prefix hashes. Each request's prefix hash is matched in one cycle, so shared system-prompt KV is reused instead of recomputed and duplicated. The relays have zero off-state leakage, whereas a CMOS CAM leaks heavily at 125 C.
why: Prefix KV dedup cuts KV memory 2-10x for multi-user assistants on hot roadside or cell-tower edge servers.

title: Leak-toward-zero encoding turns thermal retention loss into harmless pruning
idea: DRAM charge leaks only one way (true cells go 1 to 0). Store neural weights in sign-magnitude with magnitude bits in true cells and the sign bit in robust NVM, so any leakage flip at 125 C can only shrink a weight's magnitude, which acts like gentle pruning. Error-tolerant tensors then live in banks with 4-8x relaxed refresh.
why: Recovers refresh bandwidth and energy (fact 3) and removes the guard-band overprovisioning hot designs carry. Expect ~20-30% less DRAM for the same delivered bandwidth.

title: Johnson-noise Morris counters shrink telemetry and tiering tables tenfold
idea: Replace exact 32-bit counters in flow tables, feature-frequency tables and page-hotness tables with 4-bit probabilistic Morris counters. Each one increments with probability 2^-c, decided by a comparator on amplified resistor thermal noise. Johnson noise grows with temperature, so the entropy source improves at 125 C rather than degrading.
why: Counting and telemetry structures in hot edge gateways shrink 8-10x, freeing DRAM.

title: Carbon-nanotube van der Waals memory runs code and weights in place
idea: Use CNT-fabric memory, which switches by van der Waals contact and is projected to retain data over 10 years well above 125 C, as byte-addressable main storage. OS images, maps and model weights then execute in place, removing the duplicate copy that is loaded from flash into DRAM at boot.
why: Eliminates the storage-to-DRAM double copy, for 40-60% less DRAM in ECUs plus instant-on.

title: Adiabatic reversible logic makes recomputing activations cheaper than storing
idea: Run on-device adaptation with reversible network layers (RevNet-style) on charge-recovery adiabatic logic. Activations are recomputed backward from outputs at ~10x less switching energy, so they are never stored. Adiabatic switching also cuts self-heating, keeping junctions inside budget at 125 C ambient.
why: On-device fine-tuning memory falls 5-10x because activations are not stored.

title: Repurpose automotive embedded-PCM lines as U.S. weight-memory chiplets
idea: Ge-rich GST embedded PCM, whose crystallization temperature has been raised for 150 C automotive MCUs at 28/18 nm, is sold as stand-alone read-mostly weight chiplets. They are built on underused mature-node lines without EUV and hybrid-bonded under NPUs, and DRAM is reserved for activations and KV.
why: Moves read-mostly bits off scarce DRAM onto mature, U.S.-capable capacity, at far lower capital per bit than a DRAM fab (fact 4).

title: Fused-silica diffractive plate performs the first vision layers optically
idea: Etch a learned phase mask into fused silica, which is stable far above 125 C, in front of each camera sensor. The first convolutional layers then happen as diffraction before photons reach the pixels, and the sensor outputs feature maps directly. Neither those weights nor their large early activations ever touch DRAM.
why: Early layers create the largest activation tensors, so removing them cuts ADAS vision DRAM 3-5x.

title: Ferroelectric fast checkpoints let exclusive tasks time-share one DRAM
idea: Mutually exclusive vehicle workloads (parking, highway, cabin assistant) each checkpoint their whole state into AlScN FeRAM in milliseconds, using ns polarization switching. The next task is then swapped in, so one small DRAM serves several tasks over time instead of each owning its own. Wurtzite polarization survives 125 C for 10 years.
why: DRAM is sized for the peak task rather than the sum, for 2-4x less DRAM per vehicle.

title: AlN resonator spectra read hundreds of ROM bits per wire
idea: Encode tokenizer, embedding and activation lookup tables as the mass-loading of AlN bulk-acoustic resonators, each tuned to a distinct frequency. One RF sweep on a shared line reads hundreds of resonators at once from their spectral peaks, so no row decoders are needed. A reference resonator cancels the ~-25 ppm/C temperature drift, and frozen mass-loads do not change at 125 C.
why: A dense, decoder-free ROM for static lookup data attacks periphery (fact 7) and moves MB-scale tables out of DRAM in edge devices.

title: Microheater-gated zirconia ionic memory hosts shared read-mostly pages
idea: Store deduplicated read-only pages (shared libraries, model weights, map tiles) in yttria-stabilized zirconia cells. Their oxygen-ion motion is frozen at 125 C but fast at ~400 C, so writes use a local microheater pulse and the hot ambient cannot disturb the data. Reads are fast and resistive.
why: Thermal write gating gives 10-year retention at 125 C, and one shared physical copy serves all processes and VMs, cutting DRAM 20-40%.

title: Heat-annealed self-healing flash becomes a write-tolerant DRAM extension
idea: Use the 125 C ambient plus brief on-die heater pulses to keep annealing trapped charge out of NAND tunnel oxide (the self-healing flash effect), pushing SLC endurance toward 1e8 cycles. Flash can then act as a swap tier for warm pages behind a small DRAM.
why: Turns heat from enemy into feature: DRAM can shrink 2-4x behind a high-endurance flash tier in hot environments.

title: Random-telegraph-noise dither enables unbiased 2-bit KV caches
idea: Quantize KV values to 2 bits with stochastic rounding, which keeps the expectation unbiased. The random bits come from single-trap random telegraph noise in minimum-size transistors. Trap switching speeds up at 125 C, so the entropy source gets better with heat over the 10-year life.
why: 2-bit KV with near-4-bit accuracy cuts KV memory 8x versus FP16.
